For a buyer the practical points are the form bought, the basis a result is reported on, where the potatoes came from and the laboratory’s reporting limit. Testing finds contamination but does not remove it.



<a id="ingredient-identity-and-scope"></a>
## What counts as potatoes

<a id="hmi-ing-001"></a>
<a id="what-commodity-biological-species-edible-part-and-commercial-forms-does-this-page-cover"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-002"></a>
<a id="which-processing-states-and-derivatives-are-distinct-materials-rather-than-synonyms"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-003"></a>
<a id="what-evidence-can-be-transferred-between-those-materials-and-what-requires-a-separate-answer"></a>

This page covers potatoes in 7 forms kept separate in every comparison: potatoes, as sold (1,141 results), potatoes, peeled or flesh (66 results), potatoes, cooked (58 results), potatoes, flour or meal (24 results), potatoes, dried (16 results), potatoes, powder or ground (6 results) and potatoes, canned (3 results).<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span <div class="hmi-analyte-explorer" id="hmi-occurrence-potatoes" data-analyte-explorer data-compact-intro="true" data-source-summaries="true"><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure" data-explorer-context><summary data-open-context aria-haspopup="dialog" aria-controls="hmi-occurrence-potatoes-drawer">Comparison methods and scope</summary><div data-explorer-context-content>

<p>Each row is one statistic a source reports for one form of potatoes, group and metal; percentiles, ranges and maxima reported for the same samples as a mean or median are shown on that row. Different forms and preparation states are kept apart, and dry-weight results never share a reference with as-sold or fresh-weight results. Ratings place a result against an HMI reference built from monitoring results and ordinary-setting medians for the same form and basis. Same-study contrasts compare a contaminated or treated site with its control, targeted with random sampling, a prepared form with the unprocessed one, or one group of a study with the median of its other groups. Held rows failed a check against their own source and are shown but not compared.</p>

Counts describe evidence units, not independent studies or certainty.</p><div class="hmi-drawer-table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Contributing family</th><th scope="col">Reference units</th><th scope="col">Weight</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>WHO GEMS/Food</td><td>160</td><td>25%</td></tr><tr><td>Islamoglu et al. 2021</td><td>1</td><td>25%</td></tr><tr><td>Sixto et al. 2023</td><td>6</td><td>25%</td></tr><tr><td>Stančić et al. 2016</td><td>2</td><td>25%</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Methods</p><p>HMI pools subgroup medians for potatoes, as sold on a as sold, as eaten or fresh weight basis: monitoring results summarized as one median per reporting region, sampling type and collection year, total diet composites and printed sample values as single observations, and printed subgroup medians from ordinary farms or markets. Each sampling family has equal total weight. Non-detects stay as zero-to-limit intervals, so quartiles carry lower and upper bounds. Means, ranges and maxima never enter as observations. Other forms, other bases, targeted sampling and results from mining, industrial, wastewater-affected, experimental, fertiliser or manufacturer settings are kept out of this reference.</p><p>Inverse weighted empirical CDF; midpoint at exact cumulative-weight boundaries. At least four reference units and a definitely positive Q1 to Q3 spread are required. This is a display eligibility rule, not statistical validation.</p><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Limitations</p><p>4 sampling families with different designs; none is a probability sample of world supply. Reporting regions and purchase markets are not growing areas. Non-detects with differing limits widen the bounds. <a id="sources-and-contamination-pathways"></a>
## How metals reach potatoes

<a id="hmi-ing-010"></a>
<a id="what-evidence-supports-root-uptake-surface-deposition-feed-transfer-or-other-biological-pathways"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-011"></a>
<a id="what-contamination-can-arise-from-agricultural-inputs-harvesting-processing-equipment-or-packaging"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-012"></a>
<a id="which-source-attribution-claims-are-measured-modelled-inferred-or-unresolved"></a>

The evidence on how metals reach potatoes comes from studies that compared exposed and ordinary settings. Potatoes, as sold from private garden (industrial-affected area) had lead higher at 58.8 µg/kg, against 18.5 µg/kg for private garden in the same study.<sup class="cite">[[sources/ristevska2026-north-macedonia-vegetables-lead|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Temelkovska Ristevska K, Pavlovska G, Petrović SM, Savić S, Blazhevska T, Trajkovska Petkoska A · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/ristevska2026-north-macedonia-vegetables-lead">Dietary Lead Intake from Vegetables Grown near Industrial Pollution Sources and Associated Public Health Risks: Case Studies from North Macedonia</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Pollutants 2026, 6, 58</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/ristevska2026-north-macedonia-vegetables-lead">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> In another study, potatoes, as sold from Cu100Zn100Pb100 (experiment) had Zn higher at 9,600 µg/kg, against 3,600 µg/kg for control plot, no metal addition, no fertilizer in the same study.<sup class="cite">[[sources/gromakova2017-rostov-root-crop-amendment|30]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">N. V. Gromakova · 2017</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/gromakova2017-rostov-root-crop-amendment">Yield Assessment of Beetroot and Potato, Cultivated on Ordinary Chernozem Contaminated with Heavy Metals</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Vegetable Crops of Russia 5(38):74–75</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/gromakova2017-rostov-root-crop-amendment">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

These are observational comparisons from single studies; the size of the difference depends on the site, metal and distance.

<a id="hmi-ing-024"></a>
<a id="what-costs-constraints-adverse-effects-or-failure-modes-are-documented-and-which-are-unknown"></a>

Avoiding exposed growing areas lowered the metal measured in the studies available, but no study measured the cost or supply effect of doing so.<sup class="cite">[[sources/ristevska2026-north-macedonia-vegetables-lead|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Temelkovska Ristevska K, Pavlovska G, Petrović SM, Savić S, Blazhevska T, Trajkovska Petkoska A · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/ristevska2026-north-macedonia-vegetables-lead">Dietary Lead Intake from Vegetables Grown near Industrial Pollution Sources and Associated Public Health Risks: Case Studies from North Macedonia</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Pollutants 2026, 6, 58</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/ristevska2026-north-macedonia-vegetables-lead">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Metals do not move together, so a lot that passes a lead limit says little about cadmium, arsenic or nickel unless those are tested as well.



<a id="sampling-and-testing"></a>
## Testing potatoes for metals

<a id="hmi-ing-025"></a>
<a id="what-sampling-design-is-appropriate-for-the-ingredient-heterogeneity-lot-and-decision"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-026"></a>
<a id="which-methods-species-measurements-validation-evidence-and-reporting-limits-are-needed"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-027"></a>
<a id="what-can-a-certificate-of-analysis-or-non-detect-establish-and-what-remains-untested"></a>

Results depend on the method and its reporting limit. Reporting limits for lead ranged from 0.08 µg/kg (lyu 2022) to 3,000 µg/kg (WHO GEMS/Food), so a non-detect from a less sensitive method says much less.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/lyu2022-characterizing-the-exposome-of-food-contamination-and-china|42]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">lyu · 2022</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/lyu2022-characterizing-the-exposome-of-food-contamination-and-china">Characterizing the Exposome of Food Contamination and China Total Diet Study: Project for Improving Food Safety Risk Assessment in China</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">China CDC Weekly</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/lyu2022-characterizing-the-exposome-of-food-contamination-and-china">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Reporting limits for cadmium ranged from 0.04 µg/kg (WHO GEMS/Food) to 1,000 µg/kg (WHO GEMS/Food), so a non-detect from a less sensitive method says much less.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Reporting limits for total arsenic ranged from 0.088 µg/kg (WHO GEMS/Food) to 40,400 µg/kg (WHO GEMS/Food), so a non-detect from a less sensitive method says much less.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

A useful lot result names the form, the basis and a quantification limit well below the limit that applies.

<a id="universal-faqs"></a>
## Potatoes FAQs

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="what-heavy-metals-are-found-in-potatoes" data-anchor="what-heavy-metals-are-found-in-potatoes" data-question="What heavy metals are found in potatoes?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>What heavy metals are found in potatoes?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

The library reports lead, cadmium, total arsenic, inorganic arsenic, dimethylarsinic acid, monomethylarsonic acid, total mercury, nickel, chromium, aluminium, tin, antimony, uranium, Co, Cu, Fe, Mn, Zn, V, Se, Ag, As, AsB, AsSug OH, AsSug PO4, AsSug SO3, AsSug SO4, Ba, Ca, Ga, Hg, I, K, Mg, Mo, P, Sr, Ti and Tl in potatoes, most often lead, cadmium and total arsenic.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a <details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="how-do-heavy-metals-get-into-potatoes" data-anchor="how-do-heavy-metals-get-into-potatoes" data-question="How do heavy metals get into potatoes?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>How do heavy metals get into potatoes?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

In the studies available, potatoes from contaminated or exposed settings carried more metal than potatoes from the same study’s control.<sup class="cite">[[sources/ristevska2026-north-macedonia-vegetables-lead|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Temelkovska Ristevska K, Pavlovska G, Petrović SM, Savić S, Blazhevska T, Trajkovska Petkoska A · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/ristevska2026-north-macedonia-vegetables-lead">Dietary Lead Intake from Vegetables Grown near Industrial Pollution Sources and Associated Public Health Risks: Case Studies from North Macedonia</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Pollutants 2026, 6, 58</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/ristevska2026-north-macedonia-vegetables-lead">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Potatoes, as sold from private garden (industrial-affected area) had lead higher at 23.5 µg/kg, against 18.5 µg/kg for private garden in the same study.<sup class="cite">[[sources/ristevska2026-north-macedonia-vegetables-lead|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Temelkovska Ristevska K, Pavlovska G, Petrović SM, Savić S, Blazhevska T, Trajkovska Petkoska A · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/ristevska2026-north-macedonia-vegetables-lead">Dietary Lead Intake from Vegetables Grown near Industrial Pollution Sources and Associated Public Health Risks: Case Studies from North Macedonia</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Pollutants 2026, 6, 58</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/ristevska2026-north-macedonia-vegetables-lead">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="which-regions-report-the-lowest-levels-in-potatoes" data-anchor="which-regions-report-the-lowest-levels-in-potatoes" data-question="Which regions report the lowest levels in potatoes?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Which regions report the lowest levels in potatoes?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Among GEMS/Food reporting regions, potatoes, as sold had the lowest lead subgroup median in PAHO (1.4 µg/kg) and the highest in WPRO (110 µg/kg); reporting regions are markets, not growing areas.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> For cadmium, the lowest regional median was in PAHO (4 µg/kg) and the highest in EURO (133 µg/kg).<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="does-processing-change-heavy-metals-in-potatoes" data-anchor="does-processing-change-heavy-metals-in-potatoes" data-question="Does processing change heavy metals in potatoes?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Does processing change heavy metals in potatoes?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Only comparisons between forms in the same study are available, not before-and-after measurements of the same potatoes.<sup class="cite">[[sources/efsa-lead-contam-2010|39]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">EFSA Panel on Contaminants in the Food Chain (CONTAM) · 2010</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/efsa-lead-contam-2010">Scientific Opinion on Lead in Food</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">EFSA Journal 2010;8(4):1570</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/efsa-lead-contam-2010">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Potatoes, peeled or flesh (Starchy roots and potatoes) had lead lower at 0 µg/kg, against 3 µg/kg for the unprocessed form in the same group (potatoes, as sold).<sup class="cite">[[sources/efsa-lead-contam-2010|39]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">EFSA Panel on Contaminants in the Food Chain (CONTAM) · 2010</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/efsa-lead-contam-2010">Scientific Opinion on Lead in Food</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">EFSA Journal 2010;8(4):1570</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/efsa-lead-contam-2010">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>
